Alex —

Great speaking yesterday. Per our call, attaching the initial demand profile and a quick topology sketch so we have a baseline for capacity planning. Key asks from our side to keep the implementation timeline tight:

- Confirm primary regions (you mentioned US-West and EU-North)
- Expected steady-state QPS / concurrent sessions per region (rough avg and 95th pct)
- Any regulatory requirements for EU traffic residency or data egress constraints

From Redwood's playbook we'll propose: a small latency-optimized pool for hot-model serving, a cost-optimized pool for batch/low-latency-tolerant routing, and a regional burst policy that can draw from a reserved global standby pool if regional spikes exceed thresholds.

Attachments: Initial-Demand-Profile.csv, Proposed-Topology.drawio

Thanks, got the attachments. Quick answers up front:

- Regions: US-West (primary), EU-North (secondary for EU customers). We may add APAC later but not in phase 1.
- Steady-state: ~120 QPS sustained US-West, 30 QPS EU-North; 95th percentile spikes: US-West ~380 QPS sustained bursts lasting 3-6 mins, EU ~90 QPS.
- Residency: EU user data must stay in EU region for inference logs; request that any model KV caches or telemetry be stored in-region.

Questions from our infra team: what is your recommended autoscale cooldown and prewarm node buffer for ~3-6 minute spikes? Also, what's the process for invoking the reserved global standby pool — is that automatic or manual?

I've CC'd procurement so they see the timeline. We'll aim to confirm numbers and a PO cadence by Friday.

From: Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Pool governance + burst/SLA stitch - Asteria Insights

Alex / Ben —

Thanks for the traffic profile, Alex. A few recommendations based on those spike shapes and the EU residency note:

1) Topology & pools
   - Hot pool (latency SLO  < 120ms tail): provision 3x A100-style GPUs in US-West as baseline with k8s-like autoscaling to 9 nodes on sustained increase; EU-North hot pool: 1x baseline, scale to 4 nodes.
   - Cost pool (throughput/cached inference): use quantized variants and CPU-backed batching for long-tail workloads; keep a small buffer of 2 nodes per region.

2) Autoscaling / prewarm policy (recommended)
   - Scale triggers: target 70% GPU utilization for up-scaling, 45% for downscale; use moving-window of 30s for decisions to handle 3–6 minute bursts.
   - Prewarm buffer: maintain a rolling buffer of 1 spare hot node + 1 spare cost node in US-West; EU-North buffer of 1 hot node. Prewarming happens automatically when predicted traffic (ML-based short-term predictor) crosses 60% of reserved burst threshold.

3) Reserved global standby pool & burst invocation
   - Standby pool: regional failover first; if regional capacity exhausted, requests route to the standby global pool in us-east (cold-warm nodes).
   - Invocation: automatic by policy with canary routing for first 20% of burst requests, then full route if latency/SLA metrics remain stable. Manual override available via Console and API for procurement/CS to trigger a forced burst.

4) Data residency
   - KV cache and telemetry: keep in-region for EU-North. We'll supply a tenant-scoped encryption key and audit logs for SOC2 evidence.

5) Implementation checkpoints
   - Week 1 (prep): finalize PO & SOW, confirm network peering and IP allowlists.
   - Week 2 (turnup): deploy pools in US-West + EU-North, run synthetic load tests.
   - Week 3 (cutover): route 20% traffic canary, expand to 100% over 48 hours with rollback windows.

I've attached a governance matrix draft that maps ownership and escalation lanes. Will iterate after we get any constraints from your security team.

Grace O'Connor
Director, Customer Reliability
Redwood Inference
